title: Try a Partner Dance
subtitle: Learn a few steps with another human. Looking like you know what you're doing is optional.
steps: Find a beginner partner dance class. Salsa, Lindy Hop, or CJ's pick, West Coast swing, are places to start. Check the price, start time, and whether you need a partner.
Arrive a little early and tell the instructor you're new. Wear something comfortable and follow the studio's shoe guidance. Your feet have enough to think about.
Say hello to your partner and try the steps together. Lose the beat? Rejoin when you find it. If partners rotate, you get another hello with every change.
Before you leave, ask someone when they usually come dancing. You now have a few steps and a reason to come back.

title: Join Pickleball Open Play
subtitle: Meet a few people. Chase a small plastic ball. Become briefly invested in both.
steps: Find beginner-friendly pickleball open play at a park or recreation center. Check the time, fees, and whether you can borrow a paddle.
Bring water and court shoes. Tell the organizer or a waiting player you're new and ask how to join the rotation. This is a perfectly respectable opening move.
Learn a few names and join a game at your level. Ask about rules as you go. Keeping score may briefly become a group project.
Thank your fellow ball-chasers and ask when they play again. If you had fun, put the next session on your calendar.

title: Say Hello at the Park
subtitle: The dog is your opening line. The person has the stories.
steps: Take a walk in a public park. If someone with a dog seems open to a chat, offer a hello and a sincere dog compliment. There is usually material to work with.
Ask the dog's name. If the person welcomes the conversation, introduce yourself and ask their name too. The human also gets a name.
Ask how the dog came into their life, or whether they come here often. Then listen. Follow the interesting bit instead of working through a questionnaire.
Enjoy the conversation for as long as it's welcome. Thank them for the chat when it's time to go. A short, friendly hello counts too.
safety: Ask the owner before approaching or touching their dog, and give people space if they are busy or prefer to keep walking.
